blocks.text: His face had a strong—a very strong—eagle-like shape. His thin nose had a high bridge, and his nostrils were unusually curved. His forehead was high and rounded like a dome. His hair grew thinly around his temples, but very thickly everywhere else. His eyebrows were very large and heavy, and they almost met above his nose. Their bushy hair was so thick that it seemed to curl. As far as I could see it under his heavy moustache, his mouth was set hard and looked rather cruel. His white teeth were unusually sharp, and they stuck out over his lips. His lips were remarkably red. This showed surprising energy and life for a man of his age. As for the rest of his face, his ears were pale and extremely pointed at the tops. His chin was wide and strong, and his cheeks were firm, though thin. Overall, the effect was one of extreme paleness.

Until now, I had noticed the backs of his hands as they rested on his knees in the firelight. They had seemed rather white and delicate. But now, seeing them close to me, I could not help noticing that they were rather rough. They were broad, with short, thick fingers. Strangely, there were hairs in the centre of the palm. His nails were long and thin, and cut to a sharp point. As the Count leaned over me and his hands touched me, I could not hold back a shudder. Maybe it was because his breath smelled terrible, but a horrible feeling of sickness came over me. No matter what I tried, I could not hide it. The Count clearly noticed this and drew back. He gave a grim sort of smile, showing his teeth sticking out more than he had done yet. Then he sat down again on his own side of the fireplace. We were both silent for a while. As I looked towards the window, I saw the first dim streak of the coming dawn. Everything seemed strangely still. But as I listened, I heard the howling of many wolves, as if from down below in the valley. The Count’s eyes shone brightly, and he said:—
“Listen to them—the children of the night. What music they make!” I suppose he saw an expression on my face that seemed strange to him, and he added:—
“Ah, sir, you people who live in the city cannot understand the feelings of the hunter.” Then he stood up and said:—

“But you must be tired. Your bedroom is all ready, and tomorrow you may sleep as late as you like. I have to be away until the afternoon, so sleep well and dream well!” With a polite bow, he opened the door to the eight-sided room for me himself, and I entered my bedroom....
I am in a sea of wonders. I have doubts, and I am afraid. I think strange things that I do not dare to admit to my own soul. May God protect me, if only for the sake of those who are dear to me!

7 May.—It is early morning again, but I have rested and enjoyed the last twenty-four hours. I slept until late in the day and woke up on my own. When I had got dressed, I went into the room where we had eaten supper. I found a cold breakfast laid out. There was also coffee, kept hot because the pot had been placed by the fire. There was a card on the table with these words written on it:—

“I have to be away for a while. Do not wait for me.—D.” I began eating and enjoyed a good, filling meal. When I had finished, I looked for a bell so that I could tell the servants I was done. However, I could not find one. There are certainly strange things missing in this house, especially when I think of all the extraordinary signs of wealth around me. The plates and dishes on the table are made of gold. They are so beautifully made that they must be worth a huge amount of money. The curtains, the cloth covering the chairs and sofas, and the curtains around my bed are made of the most expensive and most beautiful materials. They must have been worth a fortune when they were made. They are centuries old, yet they are still in excellent condition. I saw similar ones in Hampton Court, but there they were worn out, torn at the edges, and full of moth holes. Even so, there is not a single mirror in any of the rooms. There is not even a small mirror on my table. I had to take the little shaving mirror from my bag before I could shave or brush my hair. I have not seen a servant anywhere yet, and I have not heard any sound near the castle except the howling of wolves. Some time after I finished my meal—I do not know whether to call it breakfast or dinner, because I ate it between five and six o’clock—I looked around for something to read. I did this because I did not want to walk around the castle until I had asked the Count’s permission. There was nothing at all in the room—no book, no newspaper, not even anything to write with. So I opened another door in the room and found a sort of library. I tried the door opposite mine, but it was locked.
